fields.summary: 2026-11-15, after milestone 38's change sets merged. The orchestrator reported milestone 38's measurements at a98fd40: a clean cold make test on a quiet box took 423 s wall for 967 CPU-s (570 user + 397 sys, 228% CPU) against the 4-minute target (baseline 854 s for 972 CPU-s, so milestone 38 cut waiting, not work); a warm make test took 41 s (target 60 s, met); nothing was lost (1,948 tests and 398 txtar files against 1,892 and 395); there were too few PR CI runs since #588 to call the CI median. The owner asked what the projection is and how it would affect performance. The orchestrator measured this repo's log (24,560 entries, 127 MB): rhiza status 2.0 s, rhiza inbox 2.3 s, rhiza check 15.3 s, rhiza version 14 ms. The owner saw refactoring and architectural opportunities, so the orchestrator ran a read-only architecture survey (~/orchestrator/architecture-survey-2026-11-15.md). Its main finding: much of the projection already exists as internal/index, which production writes and many reads use; the interim model (internal/api/model.go newModel) that folds the whole log survives as a fallback and is what internal/api's tests run on; the model rules are implemented three times (the interim model, the strict engine in internal/model, and a hybrid in write_indexed.go); status (also the hook op), render, change ls, the inbox fallback, the daemon fold and check still fold the whole log; check rebuilds the as-is model about 96 times (model.WhatIf twice per in-flight change set) over a serial decode; cmd/rhiza's scripts re-execute the test binary for every rhiza line (about 5,330), though AGENTS.md says they run in-process. The orchestrator proposed a milestone, 'Reads come from the projection', of four change sets in this order: a parity harness with internal/api tests on the index; check without the repeated what-if rebuilds; finishing the projection (one projection interface, the index its only implementation with pending entries overlaid, the interim model deleted, status, render, change ls and the daemon fold moved onto it); and rhiza run in-process in the scripts. Two items come later: moving the daemon, run, ship and web application code out of internal/api, and investigating what fills the 127 MB log. The owner agreed to that scope, agreed that the strict engine is the spec when the parity test finds a disagreement, chose autonomous planning, and closed milestone 38 with the cold time as an interim result, its target moving to the new milestone. Left to the orchestrator as arbiter: the new milestone's command-latency and check targets and the measuring commands.
